newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Mayne sees higher 96/97 net profit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Mayne sees higher 96/97 net profit.

text.p: Transport, telecommunications and healthcare group Mayne Nickless Ltd said on Monday it expected to post an improved net profit figure for the year ended June 30, 1997.
"We think we'll improve this year. Certainly we've budgeted for an improvement in the bottom line this year," managing director, Bob Dalziel, told reporters.
Dalziel also said he did not expect the group to make any major abnormal write-offs over fiscal 1996/97.
Dalziel said the company aimed to achieve solid profit growth in the years following fiscal 1996/97.
"What we're looking for is to have our base right this year and we're seeking short-term growth but we're seeing long-term sustainable returns improving in the 1997/98 year," he said.
Mayne's net profit for the year to June 30 was A$11.55 million, down from A$79.23 million a year earlier.
The company also reported A$108 million worth of abnormal losses.
Its bottom line was hit mainly by a surge in interest and tax expenses.
Mayne had pegged its future profit growth on a restructure of its Belgium logistics and Australian express businesses.
The Heijden Logistic unit in Belgium performed poorly over the year due to an inappropriate product and customer mix Dalziel said.
"It will probably take us at least another six to nine months to resolve the key issues, but we expect it to be in a profitable circumstance but the end of this financial year," he added.
Work also had begun on revamping the Australian IPEC Road express transport division, which also helped dragged full year profits lower.
"Key steps have been within the last three months to improve our profitability but significantly more work has to be done over the ensuing six months," Dalziel said.
Dalziel said the company would elaborate on the unit's progress in early 1997.
Healthcare were still expected to dominate future earnings growth and would receive the largest share of funds earmarked for future investment.
The company was not concerned by the short-term implications of a rise in health insurance premiums on its healthcare businesses.

"We've managed the situation quite well because most of our hospitals happen to be in areas where the level of insurance is probably in the 60 or 70 percent territory," Mayne chief financial officer Shane Tanner said.
